quiz.prompt: Removing items from a List inside a foreach over that same list...
choices: works, removing every match
skips every other item silently
throws InvalidOperationException
throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException
quiz.explanation: List<T> keeps a version number that every Add or Remove increments, and its enumerator compares that number on each MoveNext. After the first Remove, the next step of the foreach sees a changed version and throws with "Collection was modified". It never silently skips items, and no index goes out of range. Use RemoveAll(predicate), loop backwards by index, or iterate a copy made with ToList().

quiz.prompt: What does `new HashSet<int> { 1 }.Add(1)` return?
choices: `true`
`false`
It throws
quiz.explanation: HashSet<T>.Add returns a bool that reports whether the value was inserted. The set already holds 1 from the collection initialiser, so the second add finds an equal element, leaves the set unchanged and reports that. A duplicate is not an error, so nothing throws, and Add returns a flag rather than the element, so the result is never 1.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a string-keyed Dictionary match keys case-insensitively?
choices: Calling ToLower() on each key when it is looked up
Using a SortedDictionary, which compares keys ignoring case
Nothing: string keys compare ignoring case by default
Constructing it with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase
quiz.explanation: A Dictionary hashes and compares keys through its IEqualityComparer, and the default one for string is case-sensitive. A comparer passed to the constructor replaces both the hash code and the equality test, so "Pen" and "pen" land on one entry. Lower-casing only at lookup misses keys stored in another case, and a SortedDictionary sorts with a case-sensitive comparer by default.

quiz.prompt: You check 10,000 ids against a list of 10,000 allowed ids. What is the better data structure for the allowed ids?
choices: A HashSet<int>
A List<int>
A Queue<int>
A LinkedList<int>
quiz.explanation: Each lookup in a HashSet<int> hashes the id and checks one bucket, so 10,000 checks cost about 10,000 steps. List.Contains compares against the elements one by one, up to 10,000 per check, which is up to 100 million comparisons in total. A Queue or a LinkedList searches linearly as well and adds nothing for membership. Build the set once, outside the loop.

quiz.prompt: A method returns its private list as `IReadOnlyList<T>`. The class then adds an item. What does a caller holding the view see?
choices: The old count: the view is a snapshot copy
An InvalidOperationException on the next read
The new item: the view shares the same list
The new item once AsReadOnly() is called again
quiz.explanation: Returning a List<T> as IReadOnlyList<T> is only a conversion: the caller holds a reference to the very same list, with the writing members hidden by the interface type. When the class adds an item, the caller's next Count or loop sees it. Nothing is copied, a read never throws, and AsReadOnly is a wrapper over the same list too. For a snapshot, return a copy such as ToList().

quiz.prompt: Is the enumeration order of a Dictionary<TKey, TValue> guaranteed?
choices: Yes: it always follows insertion order
Yes: it is sorted by the keys' hash codes
No: it is shuffled randomly on each enumeration
No: it is an implementation detail
quiz.explanation: The documentation leaves the order of a Dictionary undefined. The current implementation stores entries in an array in insertion order, so small tests often look ordered, but a removal frees a slot that the next Add reuses, and the order changes. It is not sorted by hash code, and it is not reshuffled per enumeration either. Use SortedDictionary, or sort with OrderBy, when order matters.

quiz.prompt: Why is `TryGetValue` preferred over `ContainsKey` followed by the indexer?
choices: It does one hash lookup instead of two
ContainsKey allocates on each call
It takes a lock, so it is thread-safe
It caches the value for later lookups
quiz.explanation: ContainsKey hashes the key and searches its bucket, and the indexer then repeats exactly that work to fetch the value. TryGetValue searches once and hands back both the answer and the value through an out parameter. Neither method allocates or caches anything, and neither makes the dictionary thread-safe, so those are not the reason. A miss simply returns false instead of throwing.

quiz.prompt: Several request threads add to the same Dictionary. What should you use?
choices: A Dictionary marked readonly
A List of pairs instead
ConcurrentDictionary, or a lock
A [ThreadStatic] Dictionary
quiz.explanation: Dictionary assumes one writer at a time. Two threads inserting at once can both resize the bucket array or link entries into the same chain, which corrupts its internal state: entries go missing, or later calls fail. readonly only stops the field from being reassigned, a List of pairs has the same problem, and [ThreadStatic] gives each thread its own dictionary, so the threads no longer share the data.

flashcards.back: The indexer throws KeyNotFoundException for a missing key; TryGetValue returns false and sets the out value to default.
Add throws when the key exists; assigning through the indexer adds or overwrites.

flashcards.front: How do you remove items while iterating a List?
flashcards.back: Use RemoveAll with a predicate, iterate a copy, or walk the indexes backwards.

flashcards.front: What does HashSet.Add's return value tell you?
flashcards.back: Whether the value was new; false means it was already in the set.

flashcards.front: How do you make string keys case-insensitive?
flashcards.back: Construct the Dictionary or HashSet with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.
No, it is a read-only view; changes by the owner show through. Copy it for a snapshot.

flashcards.front: Why never mutate a dictionary key object?
flashcards.back: Its hash code changes, so the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can no longer be found.

flashcards.front: Which collections are safe for concurrent writes?
flashcards.back: The System.Collections.Concurrent types such as ConcurrentDictionary; the ordinary collections need a lock.

topics.title: LINQ & deferred execution
topics.summary: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy and friends; deferred versus immediate execution, multiple enumeration, First versus Single versus FirstOrDefault, empty-sequence aggregates, and IEnumerable versus IQueryable.
topics.lesson:
## A pipeline over sequences

```csharp
var topCustomers = orders
    .Where(o => o.Status == "paid")
    .GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
    .Select(g => new { CustomerId = g.Key, Total = g.Sum(o => o.Total) })
    .OrderByDescending(x => x.Total)
    .ThenBy(x => x.CustomerId)
    .Take(10)
    .ToList();
```

Each operator takes a sequence and returns a new one, so the steps read top to bottom like the sentence they implement: paid orders, grouped per customer, summed, ranked, the first 10. Filtering first keeps the later steps small. Only the final `ToList()` runs the chain; every step before it just describes work.

## Deferred execution

Most LINQ operators do **not** run when you call them. They build a query that runs when you **enumerate** it (`foreach`, `ToList`, `Count`, `First`, ...):

```csharp
var nums = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
var big = nums.Where(n => n > 1);   // nothing has run yet
nums.Add(4);
big.Count()                          // 3: the query sees the item added later
```

Consequences:
- **Multiple enumeration** runs the whole pipeline again each time: calling `Count()` and then `foreach` on the same query evaluates every lambda twice. Against a database query, it runs the SQL twice.
- Exceptions inside a lambda appear at enumeration time, possibly far from where the query was written.
- Captured variables are read at enumeration time.

`ToList()` / `ToArray()` / `ToDictionary()` execute immediately and give a **snapshot**. Materialise once when you will use a result several times or return it from a method.

## Picking one element

| call | 0 elements | 1 | 2+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `First()` | throws | first | first |
| `FirstOrDefault()` | default | first | first |
| `Single()` | throws | the one | throws |
| `SingleOrDefault()` | default | the one | throws |

All the throws are `InvalidOperationException`. Use `Single` when duplicates mean corrupted data (lookup by a unique key); `FirstOrDefault` when "none" is a normal outcome.

## Aggregates on empty sequences

`Sum()` of an empty sequence is `0`, but `Average()`, `Min()` and `Max()` of an empty sequence of non-nullable numbers throw `InvalidOperationException`. Over nullable numbers they return `null`. Guard with `Any()` or use `DefaultIfEmpty()`.

`Count()` and `Any()` are safe on empty input: 0 and `false`. With `DefaultIfEmpty(0)` the empty case becomes a one-element sequence, so `Average()` returns 0 instead of throwing; whether 0 is the right answer for "no orders yet" is a business decision, not a technical one.

## Other operators worth knowing

- `Any()` stops at the first element: prefer it to `Count() > 0`.
- `OrderBy` is a **stable** sort; chain `ThenBy` for tie-breakers (a second `OrderBy` would discard the first ordering).
- `SelectMany` flattens; `Distinct`, `DistinctBy`, `MaxBy`, `Chunk`, `Zip`, `Skip` / `Take`.
- `ToDictionary` throws `ArgumentException` on a duplicate key; use `GroupBy` or `ToLookup` when keys repeat.

## IEnumerable versus IQueryable

`IEnumerable<T>` LINQ runs your lambdas in memory. `IQueryable<T>` (EF Core's `DbSet`) translates the expression tree into SQL. Calling `.AsEnumerable()` or `.ToList()` too early pulls every row into memory and filters there (topic 20). Keep filters, ordering and paging on the `IQueryable` until the final `ToListAsync()`.

quiz.prompt: `var big = nums.Where(n => n > 1);` then `nums.Add(4);` with nums initially [1, 2, 3]. What is `big.Count()`?
quiz.explanation: Where returns a query object, not a filtered copy: the lambda has not run when big is assigned. Count() enumerates nums as it is at that moment, [1, 2, 3, 4], and three of those elements pass the filter. Answering 2 assumes Where filtered eagerly before the Add, and 4 would count every element as if there were no filter. Materialise the query where you want a snapshot.

quiz.prompt: What does `new List<int>().First()` do?
choices: Returns 0, the default value for int
Throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException
Throws InvalidOperationException
Returns -1 to signal that there is no element
quiz.explanation: First requires at least one element and throws InvalidOperationException ("Sequence contains no elements") on an empty sequence. FirstOrDefault is the variant that returns default(int), which is 0; nothing returns -1, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException is the indexer's error, not First's.

quiz.prompt: What does `new List<int> { 1, 2 }.SingleOrDefault()` do?
choices: Returns 1, the first element
Throws ArgumentException
Returns 2, the last element
Throws InvalidOperationException
quiz.explanation: SingleOrDefault returns default for an empty sequence but throws InvalidOperationException when there is more than one element, because "single" is the point of it. Use FirstOrDefault when any element will do; Single never quietly picks the first or the last.

quiz.prompt: What is `new List<int>().Sum()` and `new List<int>().Average()`?
choices: 0 and an InvalidOperationException
0 and double.NaN
An InvalidOperationException for both
0 and a DivideByZeroException
quiz.explanation: The sum of no numbers is well defined: adding nothing to 0 leaves 0. An average divides that sum by the count, and with no elements there is no meaningful result, so Average over non-nullable numbers throws ("Sequence contains no elements"). It does not return double.NaN, and because it checks the count before dividing, no DivideByZeroException occurs. Over int? the average of nothing is null.

quiz.prompt: A query is enumerated with `Count()` and then with `foreach`. How many times do its lambdas run?
choices: Once: the first enumeration caches the results
Twice: each enumeration reruns the pipeline
Three times: once when it is built, then once per run
Once: Count() reads a stored count, not the lambdas
quiz.explanation: A LINQ query stores only the steps, not results. Count() walks the source through the pipeline once, and foreach starts a fresh enumerator that walks it again, so every Where or Select lambda runs on both passes. Nothing caches between enumerations, building the query runs no lambda at all, and a filtered query has no stored count for Count() to read. Call ToList() once and reuse the list.

quiz.prompt: Which call takes a snapshot of the results right away?
choices: `Where`
`Select`
`ToList`
`OrderBy`
quiz.explanation: ToList enumerates the source immediately and copies every element into a new List<T>, so later changes to the source do not reach it. Where and Select return lazy iterators that do no work until something enumerates them. OrderBy is deferred too: it sorts only when the first element is requested, and it sorts the source as it is at that moment.

quiz.prompt: How do you sort by Total descending, then by Name for ties?
choices: `.OrderByDescending(x => x.Total).OrderBy(x => x.Name)`
`.OrderBy(x => x.Total).ThenBy(x => x.Name)`
`.OrderByDescending(x => x.Total).ThenByDescending(x => x.Name)`
`.OrderByDescending(x => x.Total).ThenBy(x => x.Name)`
quiz.explanation: OrderByDescending sets the primary key, and ThenBy adds a secondary key that is consulted only when two totals are equal. A second OrderBy starts a new sort of the whole sequence by Name alone and loses the Total order, because each OrderBy replaces the previous ordering instead of refining it. ThenByDescending would put tied names from Z to A, and ascending order on Total puts the smallest first.

quiz.prompt: Why prefer `Any()` over `Count() > 0`?
choices: Any() stops at the first element; Count() may read all
Count() runs the whole query twice, once for each comparison
Any() locks the source, so it is thread-safe
They differ: Count() > 0 ignores null elements
quiz.explanation: Any() stops at the first element, while Count() must walk the whole sequence or run a full COUNT query, so Any() is much cheaper for lazy sequences and database queries. `Count() > 0` runs the query once, not twice, and both treat null elements the same.

quiz.prompt: `orders.ToDictionary(o => o.CustomerId)` when a customer has two orders...
choices: keeps the first order and skips the rest
keeps the last order, overwriting earlier ones
throws ArgumentException for the duplicate key
groups both orders into a list for that key
quiz.explanation: ToDictionary needs unique keys and throws ArgumentException the moment a second order with the same CustomerId arrives. Use GroupBy or ToLookup when keys can repeat. It never silently keeps the first or the last value, and it does not group values into lists.

quiz.prompt: Calling `.ToList()` on an EF Core `DbSet` before `.Where(...)`...
choices: has no effect: EF still translates the Where
loads every row into memory and filters in C#
is required: a DbSet cannot be filtered
makes the filter faster by caching the table
quiz.explanation: A DbSet is an IQueryable: operators applied to it are collected into an expression tree and translated to SQL when the query runs. ToList() runs it at once as a SELECT of the whole table, and the Where that follows is Enumerable.Where over the loaded list, filtering in C#. EF translates nothing after that point; filtering a DbSet directly is the normal case, and no table caching happens.

flashcards.back: A LINQ query does no work when built; it runs each time it is enumerated, reading its source and captured variables at that moment.
To run the query once and keep a snapshot, so later reuse neither repeats the work nor sees later changes to the source.

flashcards.front: First, FirstOrDefault, Single and SingleOrDefault on an empty sequence
flashcards.back: First and Single throw; the OrDefault variants return the default value.
When more than one match would mean bad data, such as a lookup by a unique key.
Sum gives 0; Average, Min and Max throw for non-nullable numbers and return null for nullable ones.

flashcards.front: Any versus Count greater than zero
flashcards.back: Any stops as soon as it finds one element; Count may walk the whole sequence or run a counting query.

flashcards.front: Why ThenBy and not a second OrderBy?
flashcards.back: ThenBy breaks ties within the first ordering; a second OrderBy discards it and re-sorts everything.
IEnumerable runs lambdas in memory; IQueryable translates the query, for example into SQL, so filters belong on it before materialising.

topics.title: Delegates, lambdas & events
topics.summary: Func and Action, lambdas and what they capture, the for-loop capture trap, multicast delegates, events with += and -=, unsubscribing to avoid leaks, and returning an IDisposable subscription.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between `Func<int, string>` and `Action<int>`?
choices: Func runs asynchronously; Action runs synchronously
Func returns a string; Action returns nothing
Func takes a string and returns an int
Func can be stored in a variable; Action cannot
quiz.explanation: In Func<T, TResult> the last type argument is the result, so Func<int, string> takes an int and hands back a string; reading the type arguments the other way round is a common slip. Action<int> also takes an int but returns void. Both are ordinary delegate types: either can be stored in a variable or a field, and neither runs asynchronously unless the code inside it does.

quiz.prompt: `int n = 1; Func<int> f = () => n * 2; n = 5;` What does `f()` return?
choices: It does not compile
quiz.explanation: A lambda captures the variable n itself, not a copy of its value when the lambda was created, so it reads the current value 5 and returns 10. Getting 2 would need a copy taken before the assignment, such as `var copy = n;` captured instead.

quiz.prompt: The same with `foreach (var x in new[] { 0, 1, 2 }) fs.Add(() => x);` returns...
quiz.explanation: Since C# 5 each foreach iteration declares a fresh variable, so each lambda captures its own x and the functions return 0, 1 and 2. The for loop is different: it has one variable for the whole loop, which is why the earlier example returned 3, 3, 3.

quiz.prompt: A multicast `Func<int>` combines `() => 1` and `() => 2`. What does invoking it return?
choices: An array [1, 2]
quiz.explanation: Invoking a multicast delegate calls each target in order and keeps only the value of the last call; earlier results are discarded. So `() => 1` runs, then `() => 2` runs, and the invocation yields 2. Nothing adds the results up to 3, and no array is built. To collect every result, loop over GetInvocationList() and call each delegate yourself.

quiz.prompt: What can code OUTSIDE the declaring class do with an `event`?
choices: Subscribe and unsubscribe with += and -=
Invoke it as well as += and -=
Assign a new delegate with =
Read its invocation list
quiz.explanation: The event keyword restricts code outside the declaring class to += and -=. Only the class itself may invoke the event, replace its handlers with = or read the invocation list; a plain public delegate field would allow all of that, which is why events exist.

quiz.prompt: `p.Changed += (_, x) => n += x; p.Changed -= (_, x) => n += x;` Is the handler removed?
choices: Yes: lambdas with the same body compare as equal
No: the second lambda is a different delegate
It throws: that lambda was never subscribed to the event
It does not compile: lambdas cannot be removed
quiz.explanation: Delegate equality compares the target object and the method. The compiler turns each lambda expression into its own hidden method, so the second lambda, even with an identical body, points at a different method and is not equal to the subscribed one. -= finds no match and silently does nothing: removing a handler that is not in the list never throws, and the code compiles. Keep the subscribed delegate in a variable and remove that.

quiz.prompt: Why can a page that subscribes to a singleton's event leak memory?
choices: Each subscription stores a full copy of the page object
Each handler pins the page, so the GC cannot compact the heap
The singleton's handler list keeps the page reachable
Events keep the page's UI thread alive after the page closes
quiz.explanation: A subscription stores a delegate whose target is the page, so the singleton's event holds a reference to the page. The garbage collector frees only objects nothing can reach, and the singleton lives as long as the app, so every page that subscribed and never unsubscribed stays in memory with everything it references. Delegates hold references, not copies, they pin nothing, and no thread is involved. Unsubscribe when the page closes.

quiz.prompt: How do event handlers run when an event is raised?
choices: In parallel on thread-pool threads, in any order
Synchronously on the raising thread, in subscription order
Synchronously on the raising thread, newest handler first
Asynchronously, queued to run after the raising method returns
quiz.explanation: Raising an event is a synchronous call of a multicast delegate: each handler runs on the raising thread, in the order it subscribed, before the raise returns. Nothing is queued or sent to the thread pool, so a slow handler slows the code that raised the event.

quiz.prompt: Why write `Changed?.Invoke(this, n)`?
choices: So the handlers run asynchronously
So an exception in one handler is swallowed
So outside code cannot invoke the event
So raising it with no subscribers does nothing
quiz.explanation: An event field with no handlers holds null, because its delegate list is empty. Calling Invoke on null throws NullReferenceException, so `?.` checks for null and skips the call. The check also reads the field once, so a handler removed on another thread between check and call cannot cause that crash. Nothing else changes: handlers still run synchronously, an exception still propagates, and outside code still cannot invoke the event.

quiz.prompt: What is a clean way for a Subscribe method to support unsubscribing?
choices: Return an IDisposable that removes the stored handler
Return the handler count, to pass back to Unsubscribe
Set a static flag that the publisher checks before raising
Set the event to null from outside the class
quiz.explanation: An IDisposable ties unsubscribing to a pattern every C# developer knows: the caller keeps the subscription, often in a `using`, and Dispose runs code that removes exactly the delegate this Subscribe call added. A count or a static flag cannot identify one handler among many, and code outside the class cannot set an event to null at all; only the declaring class can.

flashcards.back: Func returns its last type argument, Action returns nothing, Predicate<T> is a function from T to bool.
Lambdas created in a for loop share one loop variable and see its final value; copy it into a local inside the loop.
Variables themselves, not their values at creation, and they keep the referenced objects alive.

flashcards.front: What does invoking a multicast Func return?
flashcards.back: Every target runs, and the value returned by the last one is the result.

flashcards.front: What does the event keyword restrict?
flashcards.back: Outside code can only add and remove handlers; it cannot invoke the event or replace its handler list.

flashcards.front: Why does unsubscribing a lambda written inline do nothing?
flashcards.back: Each lambda expression creates a new delegate; removal needs the same delegate that was added.

flashcards.front: How do events cause memory leaks?
flashcards.back: A long-lived publisher holds references to short-lived subscribers until they unsubscribe.
Subscribe returns an IDisposable that removes its handler when disposed, so callers can unsubscribe with using.

topics.title: Exceptions & IDisposable
topics.summary: try, catch and finally; throw versus throw ex; exception filters, inner exceptions and custom exception types; using declarations, Dispose order, and translating low-level failures without losing them.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between `throw;` and `throw ex;` inside a catch block?
choices: None: both rethrow with the original stack trace
`throw;` keeps the original stack trace; `throw ex;` resets it
`throw ex;` keeps the original stack trace; `throw;` resets it
`throw;` rethrows without the InnerException; `throw ex;` keeps it
quiz.explanation: `throw;` rethrows the exception that is already in flight and leaves its StackTrace alone, so the trace still begins at the method that failed. `throw ex;` is an ordinary throw statement: the runtime records a new trace that begins at the catch block, and the original frames are lost. Neither form touches InnerException, so the choices about InnerException describe a difference that does not exist. Use `throw;` whenever you only log and rethrow.

quiz.prompt: What does an exception filter `catch (X e) when (cond)` do when cond is false?
choices: Catches it anyway and ignores the filter result
Throws InvalidOperationException from the filter
Skips this catch; the exception keeps propagating
Rethrows it like throw ex;, resetting the stack
quiz.explanation: The runtime evaluates a filter while it searches for a handler, before any stack is unwound. A false result means this clause does not match, so the search moves on to the next clause or to the caller, exactly as if the clause were absent. Nothing is caught and rethrown, which is why the stack trace stays intact instead of being reset. A filter that itself throws counts as false; no InvalidOperationException comes out of it.

quiz.prompt: With `using var a = ...; using var b = ...;` in a method, in which order are they disposed at the end?
choices: a then b
In parallel
At the next GC
b then a
quiz.explanation: Each using declaration becomes a try/finally that covers the rest of the scope, so the one for `b` sits inside the one for `a`. At scope exit the inner finally runs first and disposes `b`, then the outer one disposes `a`. Both calls happen synchronously, one after the other, at the closing brace: nothing runs in parallel and nothing waits for the next GC. Reverse order matters because `b` may depend on `a`, like a command on its connection.

quiz.prompt: Is Dispose called when an exception is thrown inside a using block?
choices: Yes: using compiles to a try/finally block
No: the exception skips the Dispose call entirely
Yes, but later, when the GC finalises the object
No, unless it is an IAsyncDisposable with await using
quiz.explanation: using compiles to try/finally, so Dispose runs as the block is left, whether normally or by an exception. That guarantee is the whole point of using; relying on the GC's finaliser instead would release the resource at some unknown later time, if at all.

quiz.prompt: How do you add context to a low-level failure without losing it?
choices: Log it with the context, then return null to the caller
Wrap it: throw new RepositoryException("context", ex)
Rethrow it with throw ex; after logging the extra context
Set ex.Message to the extra context, then rethrow with throw;
quiz.explanation: Wrapping keeps the low-level failure attached as InnerException, so logs and debuggers still show what really went wrong, while the new message adds the context.

quiz.prompt: A method must handle FileNotFoundException with its own handler, any other IOException with a second one, and everything else with a third. Which order of catch clauses compiles and does that?
choices: catch (Exception), then catch (IOException), then catch (FileNotFoundException)
catch (FileNotFoundException), then catch (IOException), then catch (Exception)
catch (IOException), then catch (FileNotFoundException), then catch (Exception)
Any order: the runtime picks the most specific matching clause first
quiz.explanation: Clauses are tried top to bottom and the first match wins, so the most derived type goes first. A clause for a base type placed above a derived one makes the derived clause unreachable, and the compiler rejects it; the runtime never reorders clauses for you.

quiz.prompt: Why is `catch (Exception) { }` dangerous?
choices: It makes every call in the try block slower
It swallows every failure, hiding bugs as silent wrong results
It does not compile without a variable name after the Exception type
It rethrows the exception with a reset stack trace
quiz.explanation: A catch for `Exception` matches every exception type, bugs such as NullReferenceException included, and an empty body then carries on as if the call worked. The method returns a default or a half-updated state, and nobody sees an error. The clause compiles without a variable name and rethrows nothing, so the stack-trace choice is wrong, and a try block costs little when nothing is thrown. Catch only the types you can handle and let the rest reach the global handler.

quiz.prompt: When should you NOT use exceptions?
choices: For a missing database row in a GetById endpoint
For an unexpected network failure talking to a payment API
For expected, frequent outcomes like bad input in a loop
For a violated business rule that callers must handle
quiz.explanation: Throwing captures a stack trace and unwinds frames, which costs far more than returning a bool, so a loop that throws on every bad line spends most of its time in exception handling and hides the normal path. Use `int.TryParse` or a result type for outcomes you expect often. An unexpected network failure is exactly what exceptions are for, and a missing row or a broken business rule is a rare outcome that a custom exception models well.

quiz.prompt: Does the garbage collector dispose of a FileStream you forgot to close at a predictable time?
choices: Yes, as soon as the variable goes out of scope
Yes, at the next GC after the method returns
No: an unclosed FileStream is never cleaned up at all
No: finalisation timing is not deterministic
quiz.explanation: Leaving scope does nothing to an object in .NET. The handle is released only by Dispose or, if you forget it, by a finalizer, and finalizers run on their own thread at some point after a GC has found the object unreachable. Nothing says when that GC happens, so the next GC after the method returns is a guess, not a rule. The handle is usually released eventually, so the never-cleaned-up choice overstates it; until then the file stays open and may stay locked.

quiz.prompt: Who should dispose a service injected into your class by the DI container?
choices: The container that created it
Your class, in its Dispose
Nobody; the GC handles it
The caller of your class
quiz.explanation: The container tracks every disposable instance it creates. Scoped and transient ones are disposed when the scope that resolved them ends, singletons when the root provider is disposed. If your class disposed an injected service, it would break an instance other consumers may share, and the container would dispose it again later. The GC never calls Dispose, and the caller of your class did not create the service, so neither of them owns its cleanup.

flashcards.back: The bare form rethrows with the original stack trace; throwing the variable again restarts the trace at that line.

flashcards.front: What is an exception filter for?
flashcards.back: Catching only when a condition holds, such as a specific status code, without unwinding the stack when it does not.

flashcards.front: How do you add context to an exception?
flashcards.back: Throw a new, more meaningful exception and pass the caught one as its inner exception.
Dispose runs when the scope ends, even if an exception is thrown, because it compiles to try and finally.
Reverse order of declaration at the end of the enclosing scope.

flashcards.front: When are exceptions the wrong tool?
flashcards.back: For expected, frequent outcomes such as invalid user input in a loop; use Try methods or result types.

flashcards.front: Where should most exceptions be caught?
flashcards.back: Where something useful can be done, and otherwise in one global handler that logs and returns a generic error.

flashcards.front: Should you dispose services injected by DI?
flashcards.back: No. The container that created them disposes them at the end of their scope or of the application.

topics.title: async/await & Task
topics.summary: What await really does, sequential versus concurrent awaits with Task.WhenAll, async void, blocking with .Result, CancellationToken flow, exceptions from WhenAll, and async all the way down.
topics.lesson:
## What await does

```csharp
public async Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var row = await _db.Orders.FindAsync(new object[] { id }, ct);   // the thread is RELEASED while the database works
    return Map(row);
}
```

An `async` method runs **synchronously until its first await** of an incomplete task, then returns a `Task` to its caller. When the awaited operation finishes, the rest of the method continues (on a thread-pool thread in ASP.NET Core). No thread is blocked while waiting for I/O: that is why async lets a server handle thousands of concurrent requests with a few threads.

## Sequential versus concurrent

```csharp
var user  = await GetUserAsync(id);       // ~100 ms
var prefs = await GetPrefsAsync(id);      // + ~100 ms = 200 ms

var userTask  = GetUserAsync(id);         // both start now
var prefsTask = GetPrefsAsync(id);
await Task.WhenAll(userTask, prefsTask);  // ~100 ms
var (user2, prefs2) = (userTask.Result, prefsTask.Result);   // safe: both completed
```

Independent calls should start before you await them. A task starts running when the method that returns it is called, not when it is awaited, so the second call is already in flight while the first one waits. With 20 quotes at 200 ms each, awaiting them one by one takes about 4 seconds; started together they take about as long as the slowest call. Note: one `DbContext` does not support concurrent operations (topic 19); run independent database queries sequentially or use separate contexts.

## Exceptions and WhenAll

`await Task.WhenAll(a, b)` throws the **first** exception. The others are still recorded on the returned task's `Exception.InnerExceptions` (an `AggregateException`). If you need every failure, keep the WhenAll task and inspect it after the await fails. Which failure counts as first is an implementation detail: in a .NET 10 run with two tasks, the one that failed earlier in time came first, whatever the argument order. Blocking with `.Wait()` would throw the AggregateException itself; `await` unwraps it.

## Never block on async code

`task.Result` and `task.Wait()` block a thread until the task finishes. In ASP.NET Core this wastes threads and can starve the pool under load; in UI apps and old ASP.NET it deadlocks. Go **async all the way**: if a method awaits, its callers should be async too, up to the controller or handler.

## async void

`async void` methods cannot be awaited and their exceptions crash the process (there is no Task to put them in). Use `async Task`; the only legitimate `async void` is an event handler. A `try/catch` around the call cannot help: the call returns at the first await, and the exception is raised later on the synchronization context or the thread pool, where nothing catches it.

## Cancellation

Accept a `CancellationToken` in async methods and pass it to everything you await. ASP.NET Core gives you `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (bind a `CancellationToken` parameter in a minimal API or action), which is cancelled when the client disconnects, so a slow query stops instead of finishing for nobody. A cancelled operation throws `OperationCanceledException` (or its subclass `TaskCanceledException`); let it propagate.

```csharp
using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));       // a timeout on top of the caller's token
await client.GetAsync(url, cts.Token);
```

## Other tools

- `Task.Run(() => Cpu())` moves CPU-bound work to the thread pool; do not wrap I/O in it.
- `Task.WhenAny` returns the first task to complete (racing, timeouts).
- `ValueTask` avoids an allocation for methods that usually complete synchronously; await it once only.
- `SemaphoreSlim(4)` with `WaitAsync` / `Release` limits concurrency (at most four calls in flight).

quiz.prompt: Where does an async method run until its first `await` of an incomplete task?
choices: On a new thread-pool thread, right from the start
Synchronously, on the caller's own thread
Nowhere: it starts when the caller awaits it
Queued until the caller's own method returns
quiz.explanation: Calling an async method runs its body on the caller's thread, like any other call, up to the first await whose task is not yet complete. Only there does the method register the rest of its body as a continuation and hand an incomplete Task back. Nothing is moved to a thread-pool thread at the start, and nothing waits for the caller to await: the call itself starts the work. Awaiting a task that is already complete does not yield at all.

quiz.prompt: Two independent 100 ms calls awaited one after another take about...
choices: 100 ms
50 ms
It depends on the thread count
200 ms
quiz.explanation: Awaiting the first call suspends the method until that call is done, and only then does the next line start the second one, so the latencies add up to about 100 + 100 ms. The thread count changes nothing: no thread is busy during the wait, and the order of the code is what serialises the calls. To get about 100 ms, start both tasks first and await `Task.WhenAll` on them.

quiz.prompt: `await Task.WhenAll(FailA(), FailB())` where both fail. What does the await throw?
choices: The first one; the rest stay on the WhenAll task
An AggregateException holding both exceptions
Nothing; the failures stay on the WhenAll task
The exception from whichever task failed last
quiz.explanation: `Task.WhenAll` waits for every task and then faults with all of the failures collected in one list. `await` unwraps that and rethrows only the first exception in the list, so a catch block sees a single failure. The await never surfaces an AggregateException, and it never completes silently. Which failure comes first is not something to build on; to log every failure, keep the WhenAll task in a variable and read `task.Exception.InnerExceptions` in the catch block.

quiz.prompt: Why is `async void` dangerous outside event handlers?
choices: It allocates a Task on every call, so it is slower
It runs synchronously, blocking its caller until it finishes
It cannot be awaited, and its exceptions crash the app
It swallows exceptions, so failures go unnoticed
quiz.explanation: An `async void` method gives the caller nothing to await, so the caller cannot know when it finishes or whether it failed. An exception that escapes it has no Task to be stored in, so it is raised on the synchronization context, or on the thread pool when there is none, as in ASP.NET Core; unhandled there, it ends the process. It does not swallow failures, which is the opposite mistake, and the Task that `async Task` allocates is not the problem.

quiz.prompt: What is the problem with calling `GetOrderAsync(id).Result` in an ASP.NET Core controller?
choices: It returns null if the query has not completed yet
It blocks a thread while waiting, risking starvation
It does not compile: Result needs an async caller
It runs the query twice: once now and once on dispose
quiz.explanation: `.Result` blocks the calling thread until the task finishes. In ASP.NET Core that thread comes from the pool, so under load many blocked requests use the pool up and new requests queue while it grows slowly: thread-pool starvation. It compiles in a synchronous method, it never returns null early because it waits, and the query runs once. Make the action async and await the call instead.

quiz.prompt: Which token tells your code that the HTTP client disconnected?
choices: `HttpContext.RequestAborted`
`CancellationToken.None`
`new CancellationTokenSource().Token`
`IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`
quiz.explanation: The server cancels `HttpContext.RequestAborted` when the connection closes, so code that passes it to its queries and HTTP calls stops work nobody will read. `CancellationToken.None` can never be cancelled, and a token from a new CancellationTokenSource is cancelled only by whoever holds that source. `ApplicationStopping` fires when the whole host shuts down, not when one client leaves. A `CancellationToken` parameter on a handler is bound to the same token.

quiz.prompt: What does awaiting a cancelled `Task.Delay(1000, token)` throw?
choices: `TimeoutException`
`AggregateException`
`InvalidOperationException`
`TaskCanceledException`
quiz.explanation: When its token fires, `Task.Delay` completes as cancelled, and awaiting a cancelled task throws `TaskCanceledException`, a subclass of OperationCanceledException. Catch the base type in your own code, because other APIs throw OperationCanceledException itself. `await` unwraps the task, so AggregateException appears only with `.Wait()` or `.Result`. A cancellation is not a timeout either: TimeoutException comes only from code that throws it.

quiz.prompt: When is `Task.Run` appropriate in a web app?
choices: Around database calls, so they do not block the request
To turn blocking I/O code into scalable, truly async code
For CPU-bound work you want off the request thread
To run each request's handler on its own dedicated thread
quiz.explanation: `Task.Run` queues a delegate to the thread pool, which suits CPU-bound work such as resizing an image: the computation runs on a pool thread instead of inside the request code. Around a blocking database call it only moves the blocked wait to another pool thread, so nothing scales; the real async API frees the thread instead. ASP.NET Core already runs requests on pool threads, so a dedicated thread per handler buys nothing.

quiz.prompt: Can one EF Core DbContext run two queries concurrently with Task.WhenAll?
choices: No: one DbContext does not support concurrent use
Yes: each query gets its own connection from the pool
No: the second query waits until the first ends
Yes, if MultipleActiveResultSets is on in SQL Server
quiz.explanation: A DbContext is not thread-safe, and EF Core throws when a second operation starts on it before the first has finished. Await queries on one context one after another, or give each concurrent query its own context from a factory. A pooled connection per query is not how a context works.

quiz.prompt: How do you limit concurrent calls to an external API to four at a time?
choices: Task.WhenAll over the calls, which runs four at a time
A SemaphoreSlim(4), with WaitAsync and Release per call
Thread.Sleep(250) between calls to space them out
ThreadPool.SetMaxThreads(4, 4) before making the calls
quiz.explanation: `SemaphoreSlim(4)` starts with four free slots. Each call awaits `WaitAsync` before it starts and calls `Release` in a finally block when it ends, so a fifth caller waits, without blocking a thread, until a slot frees. `Task.WhenAll` sets no limit at all: it only waits for tasks that are already running. `Thread.Sleep` blocks a thread and merely spaces calls out, and `SetMaxThreads` caps pool threads, not I/O calls in flight.

flashcards.front: What does await free up while waiting for I/O?
flashcards.back: The thread: it returns to the pool and the method resumes when the operation completes.

flashcards.front: How do you run independent async calls concurrently?
flashcards.back: Start every task first, then await Task.WhenAll on them.

flashcards.front: Which exception does await Task.WhenAll throw?
flashcards.back: The first one; the full list stays on the returned task's Exception property.
They block a thread on async work, which starves the pool in servers and can deadlock in UI or legacy contexts.
Use it only for event handlers; everywhere else return Task so callers can await and observe failures.

flashcards.front: Where does a request's cancellation token come from in ASP.NET Core?
flashcards.back: HttpContext.RequestAborted, or a CancellationToken parameter on the action or minimal API handler.
Only for CPU-bound work; wrapping I/O in it adds overhead without freeing anything.

flashcards.front: How do you cap concurrency in async code?
flashcards.back: A SemaphoreSlim with the allowed count, awaited before and released after each call.

topics.title: Equality & hashing
topics.summary: == versus Equals for classes, structs, strings and boxed values; the Equals/GetHashCode contract; IEquatable<T>; why mutable keys vanish from dictionaries; double, decimal and NaN.
topics.lesson:
## Two questions: same object, or same value?

| type | `==` by default | `Equals` by default |
|---|---|---|
| class | reference (same object) | reference |
| struct | not defined unless you add it | field-by-field (via reflection: slow) |
| string | value (overloaded) | value |
| record | value (generated) | value (generated) |

```csharp
object a = 1, b = 1;
a == b        // False: == on object compares references, and these are two boxes
a.Equals(b)   // True:  Int32.Equals compares values
```

The `==` operator is chosen at **compile time** from the static types; `Equals` is virtual and dispatched at runtime. Code that compares `object` or generic `T` values must use `Equals` (or `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`).

## The contract

If you override `Equals`, you MUST override `GetHashCode` consistently:

1. Equal objects must return equal hash codes.
2. The hash code must not change while the object is in a hash-based collection.
3. Equals must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and `x.Equals(null)` is false.

Dictionary and HashSet first compare hash codes to pick a bucket, then call Equals. Break rule 1 and equal keys are not found; break rule 2 and an existing key disappears:

```csharp
var key = new Key { Id = 1 };
var set = new HashSet<Key> { key };
key.Id = 2;              // its hash changes
set.Contains(key)        // False: it sits in the bucket for the OLD hash
```

Make key types **immutable** (records are ideal).

## Implementing value equality by hand

```csharp
public sealed class Email : IEquatable<Email>
{
    private readonly string _value;
    public Email(string raw) => _value = raw.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
    public bool Equals(Email? other) => other is not null && _value == other._value;
    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => Equals(obj as Email);
    public override int GetHashCode() => _value.GetHashCode();
    public static bool operator ==(Email? a, Email? b) => Equals(a, b);
    public static bool operator !=(Email? a, Email? b) => !Equals(a, b);
}
```

`IEquatable<T>` gives collections a typed, non-boxing `Equals`. `HashCode.Combine(a, b, c)` builds a good hash from several fields. For most value objects a **record** generates all of this correctly; hand-write it only when equality is not "all fields equal" (normalised email, case-insensitive codes).

## Comparers instead of changing the type

`new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` or a custom `IEqualityComparer<T>` changes equality for ONE collection without changing the type everywhere. A comparer implements two methods, `Equals(x, y)` and `GetHashCode(x)`, and the same contract applies: equal inputs must give equal hashes, so a case-insensitive comparer must hash a case-insensitive form too. Dictionary, HashSet, `Distinct`, `GroupBy` and `ToDictionary` all accept one.

## Floating point

`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false for `double` but true for `decimal` (base-10). Use `decimal` for money. As a double, `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 has no exact base-2 form. Compare computed doubles with a tolerance, such as `Math.Abs(a - b) < 1e-9`, not with `==`. `double.NaN == double.NaN` is false, yet `double.NaN.Equals(double.NaN)` is true, so NaN keys still work in dictionaries.

## Entities versus value objects

An **entity** (an Order with an Id) is equal to itself across changes: compare by Id, never by all fields. A **value object** (Money, Email) has no identity: compare by value. Mixing the two causes duplicate rows and "the same order twice" in sets. Order 7 loaded at 10:00 with a total of 40 and again at 10:05 with 55 is still order 7. Two Money values of 5 EUR are interchangeable, whichever objects hold them.

quiz.prompt: `object a = 1, b = 1;` What are `a == b` and `a.Equals(b)`?
choices: True and True
False and True
True and False
False and False
quiz.explanation: `object a = 1` boxes the int: it copies the value into a new heap object, so `a` and `b` point at two separate boxes. Both variables are typed `object`, so `==` here is reference equality and asks whether they are one box; they are not. `Equals` is virtual, so the call reaches Int32's override, which compares the boxed numbers. A common mistake is to expect True for both, as if `==` looked at the runtime type; it does not, and .NET does not reuse boxes for small numbers.

quiz.prompt: When you override Equals, what else must you override?
choices: `ToString`
`CompareTo`
`GetHashCode`
Nothing else is required
quiz.explanation: Dictionary and HashSet use the hash code to choose a bucket and call Equals only on the items in that bucket. If Equals says two keys are equal but their hash codes differ, the lookup searches the wrong bucket and misses the key, so equal objects must return equal hashes. ToString plays no part in equality, and CompareTo belongs to ordering through IComparable, which equality does not need. The compiler warns with CS0659 when Equals is overridden alone.

quiz.prompt: A key object's Id (used by its hash code) changes after it was added to a HashSet. What does `set.Contains(key)` return?
choices: True: Contains compares by reference before it hashes
It throws InvalidOperationException: the set was modified
True: the set rehashes its items whenever they change
False: the object sits in the bucket of its old hash
quiz.explanation: A HashSet files each item under its hash code when it is added. After the Id changes, Contains computes the new hash, looks in the wrong bucket and returns false, although the object is still in the set. The set never rehashes on its own, so keep key fields immutable.

quiz.prompt: For two `class Customer` instances with identical fields and no overrides, what does `Equals` return?
choices: True: object.Equals compares all the fields
False: classes use reference equality by default
True when all of the fields are value types
It does not compile without IEquatable<T>
quiz.explanation: A class without an override inherits object.Equals, which only checks whether both references point at one object. Two `new Customer(...)` calls create two objects, so the result is false however alike the fields are. The field-by-field comparison belongs to structs, whose ValueType.Equals walks the fields, so value-type fields do not change anything for a class, and IEquatable<T> is optional. Value equality comes from records, from string's own override, or from an override you write.

quiz.prompt: Is `==` dispatched at runtime like a virtual method?
choices: Yes: == calls the runtime type's Equals
Yes for records and strings, no for others
No: the compiler picks it from the static types
No: == compares references whatever the types
quiz.explanation: Operators are static methods, so overload resolution chooses one from the declared types of the operands when the code is built. A string held in an `object` variable is compared with object's reference `==`, even though string overloads `==`: records and strings get no special treatment at runtime. It does not always compare references either, because two `string` variables use string's value `==`. Compare `object` or generic `T` values with Equals or `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`.

choices: true: decimal stores these values exactly
false: 0.1 + 0.2 rounds, as with double
It does not compile: decimal has no == operator
false: decimal is binary floating point too
quiz.explanation: decimal stores a 96-bit integer and a power-of-ten scale, so 0.1m is exactly 1 scaled by one decimal place, and the sum is exactly 0.3m. double is binary: 0.1 has no finite base-2 form, the stored values are rounded, and `0.1 + 0.2` gives 0.30000000000000004. decimal is base 10 rather than binary floating point, and it defines `==` like the other numeric types. That exactness is why money belongs in decimal.

quiz.prompt: What are `double.NaN == double.NaN` and `double.NaN.Equals(double.NaN)`?
choices: True and True
False and False
False and True
True and False
quiz.explanation: IEEE 754 says NaN compares unequal to everything, itself included, and double's `==` operator follows that rule, so `NaN == NaN` is false. `Equals` follows the object contract instead, which requires `x.Equals(x)` to be true, so it returns true. That is what lets a Dictionary with double keys find a NaN key. A common mistake is to expect the two to agree, as if they shared one rule; by design they do not.

quiz.prompt: Why implement `IEquatable<T>` on a value type or sealed class?
choices: The compiler requires it before == can be used on the type
It gives collections a typed Equals with no boxing
It lets List<T>.Sort and OrderBy compare the instances
It makes the type's hash code stable across processes
quiz.explanation: Generic collections call `IEquatable<T>.Equals(T)` when the type implements it, so a struct is compared without being boxed into object. The compiler does not require it for ==, sorting uses IComparable<T> instead, and hash codes are not stable across processes anyway.

quiz.prompt: How should two Order ENTITIES with the same Id but different totals compare?
choices: Equal: they are the same entity at different moments
Not equal: their totals differ, so the values differ
By total first, then by Id as a tie-breaker
Equal only while both are tracked by one DbContext
quiz.explanation: Entities have identity: two loaded copies of order 7 are the same order at different moments, so equality goes by Id. Comparing every value is the rule for value objects such as Money. Tracking by a DbContext changes which instance you get, not whether they are the same entity.

quiz.prompt: You need case-insensitive email uniqueness in ONE HashSet without changing the string type. What do you do?
choices: Override string.Equals in a partial class for string
Use a SortedSet<string>, which ignores letter case by default
Construct the set with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase
Use a List<string> and check Contains before each Add
quiz.explanation: An equality comparer customises equality per collection, so `new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` treats Ada@x.com and ada@X.com as one entry without touching string. A partial class cannot change string, a SortedSet compares case-sensitively by default, and List.Contains is linear.

flashcards.front: Default == and Equals for classes, structs, strings, records
flashcards.back: Classes: reference. Structs: field-wise Equals, no ==. Strings and records: value equality for both.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and the hash must stay stable while the object is in a hash collection.

flashcards.front: Why should dictionary keys be immutable?
flashcards.back: Changing a field used by the hash moves the key's hash away from its bucket, so lookups stop finding it.

flashcards.front: Why compare object or T values with Equals rather than ==?
flashcards.back: Operators are picked at compile time from static types; Equals is virtual and uses the runtime type's definition.
A strongly typed Equals that collections use without boxing value types or casting.

flashcards.front: How do you build a hash from several fields?
flashcards.back: HashCode.Combine over the same fields that Equals compares.
Entities are equal when they share identity (their id); value objects are equal when all their values match.
double is binary and cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly; decimal is base-10 and exact for money amounts.

topics.title: Memory, GC & Span<T>
topics.summary: Stack versus heap in practice, the generational GC and the large object heap, what allocates (strings, boxing, closures, LINQ), Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> for allocation-free slicing, and ArrayPool.
topics.lesson:
## Where values live (the useful approximation)

- **Locals of value types** (an `int`, a small struct) live in the method's stack frame or inside whatever contains them.
- **Objects** (class instances, arrays, strings, boxed values, closures) are allocated on the **managed heap** and cleaned up by the garbage collector.

The real rule is "value types live where their container lives": an `int` field of a class is on the heap, inside that object.

## The generational GC

New objects start in **generation 0**. A gen-0 collection is fast and frequent; objects that survive move to gen 1, then gen 2. `GC.MaxGeneration` is 2. Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go straight to the **large object heap** (collected with gen 2), so allocating big temporary arrays repeatedly is expensive.

Most objects die young, which is why short-lived allocations are cheap but not free: every allocation brings the next collection closer, and in a busy API, allocations per request translate directly into GC pauses and CPU.

## What allocates, often unnoticed

- **Strings**: every `Substring`, `Split`, `+`, `ToLower`, `string.Format` creates new strings.
- **Boxing**: putting a value type into `object` or a non-generic interface (`ArrayList`, `string.Format("{0}", 42)` in old APIs, `IComparable` on a struct).
- **Closures**: a lambda that captures locals allocates a closure object (and a delegate).
- **LINQ**: iterators and delegates per call; fine in normal code, avoidable in hot loops.
- **params arrays**, `ToList()` copies, async state machines for methods that actually await.

Measure before optimising: `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()`, BenchmarkDotNet with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, or `dotnet-counters`.

## Span<T>: a view, not a copy

`Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` represent a contiguous slice of memory (an array, a string, stack memory) without copying it:

```csharp
ReadOnlySpan<char> s = "2026-11-04".AsSpan();
int year  = int.Parse(s[..4]);        // no Substring, no new string
int month = int.Parse(s.Slice(5, 2));

var arr = new[] { 10, 20, 30 };
Span<int> tail = arr.AsSpan(1);
tail[0] = 99;                         // writes through: arr is now [10, 99, 30]

Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[256];   // stack memory, no heap allocation
```

Spans are **ref structs**: they can live only on the stack, so they cannot be fields of classes, be captured by lambdas, or live across `await`. For those cases use `Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>`, which can be stored and sliced the same way.

Most parsing APIs (`int.Parse`, `DateOnly.TryParse`, `Utf8JsonReader`, `string.Split` successors) accept spans.

## Reusing buffers

`ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(size)` hands out an array of AT LEAST that size from a pool; `Return` it when done (and never use it afterwards). It avoids allocating a new large buffer per request for things like stream copies and compression. Buckets are powers of two, so `Rent(1000)` returns a 1,024-element array: keep the length you asked for next to it. Returned arrays are not cleared by default, so pass `clearArray: true` to `Return` when the buffer held tokens or personal data.

## When to care

For typical CRUD endpoints, database round-trips dominate and allocation tuning is irrelevant. It matters in hot paths: parsing large files, serialisation, middleware that runs on every request, and high-throughput services. Clarity first; Span where a profiler says so. One 20 ms database round-trip costs more than many thousands of small allocations, so a request that makes 40 queries gains nothing from removing a `Substring`. Fix the queries, measure again, and reach for spans and pooling only where the numbers still point at allocation.

quiz.prompt: In which generation does a newly allocated small object start?
choices: Gen 2
The large object heap
Gen 0
Gen 1
quiz.explanation: The allocator hands out small objects from the gen-0 budget, filling it by bumping a pointer, so every new small object is gen 0. A gen-0 collection examines only those young objects; the ones still referenced are promoted to gen 1 and, if they survive again, to gen 2. Gen 2 holds long-lived survivors and is never where a new small object starts, and only objects of 85,000 bytes or more skip gen 0 for a separate heap for large objects.

quiz.prompt: Where is a `new byte[100_000]` allocated?
choices: Gen 0 of the small object heap
The current thread's stack
The large object heap
Unmanaged memory outside the GC heap
quiz.explanation: Any object of 85,000 bytes or more is allocated on the large object heap instead of in gen 0, and a byte array of 100,000 elements is about 100,000 bytes. The LOH is collected only together with gen 2 and is not compacted by default, which is why big temporary buffers are expensive. An array is a reference type, so it never lives on the thread's stack, and it is managed memory, not unmanaged.

quiz.prompt: Which of these allocates on the heap?
choices: `int x = 5;`
`object o = 5;`
`Span<int> s = stackalloc int[3];`
quiz.explanation: Assigning an int to an `object` variable boxes it: the runtime allocates a new box on the heap, copies the 5 into it and stores a reference to that box. `int x = 5` stays a plain value in the local, and `(1, 2)` is a ValueTuple, a struct, so it allocates nothing either. A common mistake is to count stackalloc as a heap allocation; it reserves memory in the current stack frame, which is released when the method returns.

quiz.prompt: `int.Parse("2026-11-04".AsSpan()[..4])` versus `int.Parse(s.Substring(0, 4))`: what is the difference?
choices: The span version parses without allocating a new string
They compile to the same code after JIT inlining
The span version copies the four chars to the stack
Substring shares memory with the original, so neither allocates
quiz.explanation: `AsSpan()[..4]` is a ReadOnlySpan<char> that points at the first four chars of the existing string, and int.Parse has an overload that reads a span directly, so no string is created. `Substring(0, 4)` copies those chars into a new string object on every call: a .NET string never shares memory with the string it came from. JIT inlining does not remove that allocation, and the span version copies nothing, to the stack or anywhere else.

quiz.prompt: `var arr = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }; var t = arr.AsSpan(1); t[0] = 9;` What is arr now?
choices: It throws
quiz.explanation: `AsSpan(1)` creates a view that starts at index 1 of the same array, so the span's index 0 is the array's index 1. Writing through the span stores the value straight into the array's memory, at the offset. A span never copies elements, so the array is not left unchanged, and an offset of 1 is within bounds, so nothing throws. Expecting the change at the array's index 0 forgets the offset.

quiz.prompt: Why can a `Span<T>` not be a field of a class or survive an `await`?
choices: It is too large to be copied into a heap object
It is a ref struct that must live on the stack
It is not thread-safe, so the compiler forbids sharing
It pins its array, and pins cannot outlive a method
quiz.explanation: `Span<T>` is declared as a `ref struct`, and the compiler keeps such a type on the stack: no class fields, no boxing, no lambda capture, and no local alive across an `await`, because an async method moves its locals into a heap state machine. The reason is safety: a span may point at `stackalloc` memory that dangles once the method returns. Size and thread safety have nothing to do with it, and an ordinary span pins nothing. Store a Memory<T> instead.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(10) is true?
choices: It returns an array of exactly 10, freshly zeroed
It returns an array of at least 10 that you must Return
It allocates the array on the stack, like stackalloc
It returns a pooled array that the GC returns for you
quiz.explanation: The shared pool keeps arrays in buckets sized in powers of two, so Rent(10) gives you an array of 16 elements: use only the length you asked for. It does not zero the array either, so a rented buffer can still hold bytes the last renter wrote. The GC knows nothing about the pool: an array you forget to hand back is just collected, and the pool allocates a new one later. Pooled arrays are ordinary heap arrays, not stack memory like stackalloc.

quiz.prompt: A lambda captures a local variable. What extra allocations can that cause?
choices: None: captured locals stay on the stack frame
A closure object for captured locals, plus a delegate
A new thread-local copy of each captured variable
A boxed copy of every local in the method, captured or not
quiz.explanation: The compiler moves captured locals into a generated closure class, so each capture costs that object plus the delegate that points at it. Only captured variables move; the other locals stay where they were, and no thread-local copies are made.

quiz.prompt: Your CRUD endpoint is slow. Where should you look first?
choices: String allocations that spans could replace
Database round-trips, missing indexes and N+1 queries
GC settings, such as server or workstation mode
Boxing in LINQ pipelines and captured lambdas
quiz.explanation: In a typical CRUD API the request spends most of its time waiting for the database. One round-trip costs milliseconds, while an allocation costs nanoseconds; an N+1 pattern multiplies the round-trips, and a missing index turns a lookup into a scan. Replacing strings with spans, removing boxing or switching between server and workstation GC trims microseconds, which is worth it only in a hot path that a profiler has pointed at.

quiz.prompt: Which tool reports allocated bytes per benchmark?
choices: BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser]
A Stopwatch wrapped around the benchmarked code
The debugger's locals window
dotnet test with code coverage on
quiz.explanation: BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser] reports allocated bytes and GC counts per operation, so you can measure an optimisation instead of guessing. A Stopwatch measures time only, and the debugger and code coverage say nothing about allocations.

flashcards.front: Value types on the stack: the precise version
flashcards.back: Value types live wherever their container lives: a local in the stack frame, a field inside its object on the heap.

flashcards.front: How does the generational GC work?
flashcards.back: New objects start in gen 0, which is collected often and cheaply; survivors move up to gen 1 and gen 2, collected less often.

flashcards.front: What is the large object heap?
flashcards.back: Where objects of 85,000 bytes or more are allocated; it is collected with gen 2, so churning big arrays is costly.
New strings from string operations, boxing, closures from capturing lambdas, LINQ iterators and delegates, and params arrays.
A view over contiguous memory (array, string or stack) that slices without copying.
Span is a stack-only ref struct for synchronous code; Memory can be stored in fields and used across await.
They may be larger than requested, must be returned to the pool, and must not be touched after being returned.
In measured hot paths such as parsing, serialisation and per-request middleware; elsewhere clarity wins.

topics.title: Dependency injection & configuration
topics.summary: The .NET service container: singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes, captive dependencies and scope validation, multiple registrations, configuration sources and their precedence, and the options pattern.
topics.lesson:
## Register, then inject through constructors

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddTransient<IPriceCalculator, PriceCalculator>();

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, IClock clock) { ... }   // the container supplies both
```

Classes declare what they need; the container builds the graph. Tests construct the same classes with fakes. Avoid the **service locator** (`provider.GetService<T>()` scattered in business code): it hides dependencies.

Constructor injection keeps every dependency visible in the signature, so a constructor with eight parameters is a sign that the class does too much. The container builds the whole graph when the outer service is requested, and a dependency nobody registered fails right then with an InvalidOperationException that names the missing type.

## Lifetimes

| lifetime | one instance per | typical services |
|---|---|---|
| Singleton | application | caches, clocks, HttpClient factories, configuration |
| Scoped | scope (one per HTTP request in ASP.NET Core) | DbContext, unit of work, the current user |
| Transient | resolution (every time it is requested) | lightweight stateless helpers |

The container disposes the `IDisposable` services it created at the end of their scope (or of the app for singletons).

## Captive dependencies

A singleton that takes a scoped service in its constructor captures ONE instance of it forever: a DbContext shared by every request and thread, leaking data between users and failing under concurrency. The container detects this when **scope validation** is on (`ValidateScopes`, enabled automatically in the Development environment by `WebApplication`): resolving throws "Cannot consume scoped service from singleton". Resolving a scoped service from the root provider is also refused. Rule: a service may only depend on services with the same or LONGER lifetime. A singleton that needs scoped work creates a scope: `using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();`.

## Several registrations

`GetRequiredService<INotifier>()` returns the **last** registration; `GetServices<INotifier>()` (or injecting `IEnumerable<INotifier>`) returns all of them, in registration order: perfect for pipelines of rules or notifiers. `TryAddSingleton` registers only if nothing is registered yet (library defaults the app can override). `GetService<T>()` returns null for an unregistered type; `GetRequiredService<T>()` throws InvalidOperationException.

## Configuration: layered sources

`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` reads, in this order (later sources override earlier ones):

1. `appsettings.json`
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json` (the environment defaults to **Production**)
3. user secrets (Development only)
4. environment variables
5. command-line arguments

Keys are hierarchical with `:` (`Smtp:Port`); in environment variables use a double underscore: `Smtp__Port=2525`. Every value is a **string** until bound. Never commit secrets to appsettings.json; use user secrets locally and environment variables or a vault in production.

## The options pattern

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<SmtpOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Smtp"));
public class Mailer(IOptions<SmtpOptions> options) { private readonly SmtpOptions _o = options.Value; }
```

`IOptions<T>` is read once (singleton); `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` re-reads per request (scoped); `IOptionsMonitor<T>` gives the current value and change notifications. Add `.ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` so a missing setting fails at startup instead of on the first email.

Because `IOptions<T>` is a singleton, a value edited in appsettings.json while the app runs never reaches it. A scoped `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` cannot go into a singleton's constructor either: scope validation rejects it like any captive dependency. Binding a section to a class with typed properties, such as `public int Port { get; set; } = 25;`, converts the strings once, in one place.

quiz.prompt: Which lifetime gives one instance per HTTP request in ASP.NET Core?
choices: Singleton
Transient
Scoped
Static
quiz.explanation: ASP.NET Core creates a DI scope for each request and disposes it when the request ends, and a scoped service gets one instance per scope, so every class in that request shares one instance. A singleton is one instance for the whole app, shared by all requests, and a transient is new on every resolution, so two classes in one request get different instances. Static is not a container lifetime at all: a static field is shared by the whole process, outside DI.

quiz.prompt: A singleton takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor. What is the problem?
choices: None: the container makes a new DbContext per request
One DbContext is captured and shared across all requests
The DbContext is disposed after the first request ends
It fails to compile: the compiler checks lifetimes
quiz.explanation: The container builds a singleton once, from the root, so the DbContext handed to its constructor is resolved once and held for the life of the app. Every request then shares that context and its change tracker, leaking state between users and failing when two threads use it at once. The container never swaps in a new context per request, and the captured context is not disposed after the first request, because the root owns it. The compiler knows nothing about lifetimes; scope validation catches this at runtime.

quiz.prompt: With ValidateScopes on, what happens when resolving a singleton that depends on a scoped service?
choices: It works, but logs a warning about the captive dependency
It returns null for the scoped dependency
It creates a new scope for the singleton automatically
It throws: cannot consume scoped service from singleton
quiz.explanation: With validation on, the provider checks the dependency chain when it builds a singleton, and a scoped service anywhere in that chain makes the resolve throw InvalidOperationException. It never logs and carries on, returns null or invents a scope, because each of those would hide the captive dependency. In the Development environment WebApplication turns this check on, together with ValidateOnBuild, so the broken registration already fails when the app is built.

quiz.prompt: Two classes are registered for `INotifier`. What does `GetRequiredService<INotifier>()` return?
choices: The first registration
The last registration
Both of them, as an IEnumerable
It throws InvalidOperationException
quiz.explanation: When you resolve a single INotifier, the container uses the newest registration for that service type, so a later registration overrides an earlier one; that is how an app replaces a library default. Several registrations are legal, so nothing throws. The first one is not preferred either: it only comes first when you ask for all of them, because `IEnumerable<INotifier>` returns every registration in registration order. GetRequiredService always returns one instance, never a sequence.

quiz.prompt: What does `TryAddSingleton<INotifier, B>()` do when `A` is already registered?
choices: Replaces A with B as the registration
Adds B alongside A, so B is now resolved
Nothing: A stays the registration
Throws: INotifier is already registered
quiz.explanation: The TryAdd methods check whether a descriptor for the service type already exists and do nothing when one does, so resolving INotifier still returns A. Libraries use them for defaults that an app overrides by registering its own type first. Replacing is what `Replace`, or `RemoveAll` followed by an Add, does, and adding alongside is what a plain `AddSingleton` does. TryAdd never throws over an existing registration.

quiz.prompt: How do you set `Smtp:Port` with an environment variable?
choices: `Smtp_Port`
`SmtpPort`
`Smtp.Port`
`Smtp__Port`
quiz.explanation: The environment-variables provider turns each `__` in a variable name into the `:` key separator, because a colon is not allowed in variable names on every platform, bash included. `Smtp__Port=2525` therefore becomes the key `Smtp:Port`. A single underscore, a dot or no separator stays part of one flat key such as `Smtp_Port`, which the Smtp section never sees. Keys are case-insensitive, so `SMTP__PORT` works as well.

quiz.prompt: appsettings.json says Port 25, an environment variable says 2525, the command line says 587. What does the app read?
choices: The first one found
quiz.explanation: WebApplication.CreateBuilder adds its sources in a fixed order: appsettings.json, the environment's file, user secrets, environment variables and the command line. When two sources set the same key, the source added later wins. The command line comes last, so it beats the environment variable's 2525 and the file's 25. Lookups do not stop at the first source found: they start from the newest source and work backwards.

quiz.prompt: What is the default environment name when ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT is not set?
choices: Development
Production
Staging
Local
quiz.explanation: When ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT (and DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT) is unset the host assumes Production, so Development-only features such as the developer exception page stay off by default. Development is set explicitly, usually by launchSettings.json during local runs.

quiz.prompt: Which options interface re-reads configuration on every request?
choices: `IOptions<T>`
`IOptionsSnapshot<T>`
`IOptionsMonitorCache<T>`
`IOptionsFactory<T>`
quiz.explanation: IOptionsSnapshot<T> is registered as scoped, so each request builds a fresh instance from the configuration as it is at that moment, and an edited appsettings.json shows up on the next request. IOptions<T> is a singleton, built once and never refreshed. IOptionsFactory<T> only creates instances when something calls it, and IOptionsMonitorCache<T> is the cache behind IOptionsMonitor<T>, which hands out the current value and raises change events instead.

quiz.prompt: What does `GetService<IMissing>()` return for an unregistered type?
choices: null, without throwing
A new default instance
It throws InvalidOperationException
It registers it
quiz.explanation: GetService returns null for a type that was never registered; GetRequiredService is the variant that throws InvalidOperationException. The container never invents a default instance and never registers anything at resolve time.

flashcards.front: Singleton, scoped and transient in one line each
flashcards.back: One for the whole app; one per scope (an HTTP request); a new one every time it is resolved.
A longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one, such as a singleton keeping one scoped DbContext forever.
A service may depend only on services with the same or a longer lifetime.

flashcards.front: How does a singleton use scoped services safely?
flashcards.back: It injects IServiceScopeFactory and creates a scope for each unit of work, resolving the scoped services inside it.
GetRequiredService gives whichever registration was added most recently; IEnumerable<T> or GetServices gives every one in registration order.

flashcards.front: Configuration precedence in a default web app
flashcards.back: appsettings.json, then the environment-specific file, then user secrets in Development, then environment variables, then the command line, each overriding the previous.
Use a double underscore where the configuration key has a colon, such as Smtp__Port.
Computed once; recomputed per request; current value plus change notifications.

topics.title: ASP.NET Core: routing & minimal APIs
topics.summary: Mapping endpoints with MapGet and friends, route templates and constraints, where parameters bind from, Results and TypedResults, route groups, and the status codes the framework produces for you.
topics.lesson:
## Endpoints

```csharp
var app = builder.Build();
```
