A 403 tells the caller the id exists, a 200 with blanked amounts still confirms it, and a 401 invites a sign-in to a tenant the user does not belong to.

quiz.prompt: What changes when the fallback policy is set to require an authenticated user?
choices: Endpoints marked [Authorize] now also need a role
Anonymous users are sent to the login page on every request
Endpoints marked [AllowAnonymous] now need a signed-in user
Endpoints with no authorization metadata now need a signed-in user
quiz.explanation: The fallback policy applies only where an endpoint declares no authorization metadata, so those endpoints now need a signed-in user. [AllowAnonymous] still opts out, and a bare [Authorize] keeps using the default policy, so no role is added. Anonymous callers of a covered endpoint are challenged on that endpoint, not redirected on every request.

quiz.prompt: A test builds `new ClaimsPrincipal(new ClaimsIdentity(claims))`, with claims but no authentication type. What is `User.Identity.IsAuthenticated`?
choices: true, because the identity carries claims
true, but only when one claim is a NameIdentifier
false: without an authentication type it is anonymous
It throws, because the authentication type is required
quiz.explanation: IsAuthenticated reports whether an authentication type was set on the identity, not whether it carries claims, so the result is false even with a NameIdentifier among the claims. The property does not throw when the type is missing. Pass a type such as "Test" to the ClaimsIdentity constructor when a test needs a signed-in user.

quiz.prompt: Where is the safest place to enforce "users see only their own tenant's orders" in a list endpoint?
choices: In the client, which hides the rows of other tenants
In the query, for example a global filter on TenantId
In a check that drops foreign rows from each loaded page
In the endpoint's [Authorize] attribute
quiz.explanation: A filter in the query keeps other tenants' rows in the database and keeps counts and pages right; a global query filter applies it to every query by default.

flashcards.back: Metadata that opens one endpoint to anonymous callers. The authorization middleware skips that endpoint entirely, even under an [Authorize] on its group or controller.

flashcards.front: What does authentication middleware do with a request that has no credentials?
flashcards.back: It leaves HttpContext.User anonymous and lets the request through; authorization decides later whether to challenge.

A requirement (IAuthorizationRequirement) names a rule as data; a handler (AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>) decides it for one request and can read the user, the resource and the endpoint's metadata. One requirement may have several handlers.
The handler base class for rules about one object: HandleRequirementAsync receives the requirement and the resource, so a rule such as 'only the creator may edit' can read the document's fields.
The policy that [Authorize] and RequireAuthorization() apply when they name no policy. Out of the box it requires an authenticated user, and AddAuthorization can replace it.
Whether the principal has a claim of its identity's role claim type with that exact value.

flashcards.front: Where must the caller's tenant come from?
flashcards.back: From a claim in the validated token or session. A tenant id in the URL, the body or a header is chosen by the caller, so it can name any tenant.
Insecure direct object reference: an endpoint acts on an id from the request without checking that the caller may access that object.

topics.title: Structured logging without secrets
topics.summary: Message templates instead of interpolated strings, positional binding of values to placeholders, what each log level is for, scopes that carry a correlation id through a request, and keeping passwords, tokens, bodies, connection strings and personal data out of logs with an allow-list at the boundary.
topics.lesson:
## Message templates, not interpolated strings

A log call takes a message template with named placeholders and the values as separate arguments:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {Country}", order.Id, order.Country);
```

The provider receives the template text unchanged plus one property per placeholder, so a log store can show every line of that template together and answer `OrderId = 42`. Placeholders bind to the arguments in order: the names in braces label the properties, and the logger never sees your variable names. An interpolated string, `$"Order {order.Id} shipped"`, is finished before the call, so the template is the rendered text, a new template for every order, with no properties to query.

## Levels say who must read the line

The levels, lowest first: `Trace`, `Debug`, `Information`, `Warning`, `Error`, `Critical`. `Information` records the normal flow (an order placed, a job finished). `Warning` is something unexpected that the code handled: a retry that then worked, a fallback, a slow dependency. `Error` is one operation that failed and needs a look. `Critical` means the app or a whole dependency is down. The ASP.NET Core templates set `"Default": "Information"` and `"Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"` in `appsettings.json`, so `Debug` lines are dropped in production unless someone lowers the minimum for one category.

## Scopes carry the correlation id

A correlation id ties together every line of one request. Middleware reads it from a header such as `X-Correlation-ID` (or generates one), echoes it in the response, and opens a scope around the rest of the pipeline:

```csharp
using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId }))
{
    await next(context);
}
```

The scope lives in an async-local slot, so it follows the request across `await` and into every class that logs during it, until the `using` ends. A provider shows scope values only when it supports scopes, and the console formatter prints them only with `IncludeScopes = true`.

## What never goes into a log

Logs are copied to other systems, kept for months and read by many people, so a secret in a log is a leaked secret. Never log passwords (a wrong password is often a typo of the right one), bearer tokens, API keys, cookies, connection strings or whole request and response bodies. Personal data (email, name, address, IP) needs a reason and a retention rule; a stable user id usually does the job: a failed sign-in line needs the user id and a reason such as `bad-password`, nothing more. Logging an object is a trap: a record's `ToString()` prints every property, so `{Request}` with a `LoginRequest(string Email, string Password)` writes the password. For a connection string, log the server and database names you parsed from it.

## Redact at the boundary: allow-list what you log

Decide at the edge what may be written, not after the fact in the log store. A deny-list hides only the names someone thought of; the day a partner sends `X-Api-Key`, it is logged in clear text. An allow-list logs known-safe fields and marks the rest. ASP.NET Core's HTTP logging works that way: it logs request and response headers but no bodies by default, and any header not in `RequestHeaders` or `ResponseHeaders` is written as `[Redacted]`. Log a body's length instead of its content.

## Exceptions and hot paths

Pass the exception as the first argument, `logger.LogError(ex, "Refund {RefundId} failed", refundId)`, so the provider stores its type, message and stack trace in the exception field. Passing `ex` as one more template argument does not set that field. Arguments are evaluated before the logger checks the level, so an expensive argument runs and its entry is then dropped; guard it with `logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)`. On hot paths, the `[LoggerMessage]` source generator writes the logging method for you: it checks the level before boxing anything, and it binds placeholders to parameter names at compile time, so a renamed parameter is a build error instead of a silently wrong property.

```csharp
[LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Warning, Message = "Retry {Attempt} for order {OrderId}")]
static partial void RetryingOrder(ILogger logger, int orderId, int attempt);
```

quiz.prompt: `logger.LogInformation($"Order {orderId} shipped")` prints the right text. What does it lose next to `logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped", orderId)`?
choices: Nothing, since both lines produce the same text and properties
An OrderId property, and one template shared by every order
Its log level, which an interpolated string resets to Debug
Thread safety, since the string is built in a shared buffer
quiz.explanation: An interpolated string is finished before the call, so the provider receives the rendered text as its template: no property to query with OrderId = 42, and a different template for each order, which breaks grouping. The level comes from the method you call, not from the string, and building the string has nothing to do with thread safety.

quiz.prompt: `logger.LogWarning("Retry {Attempt} for {OrderId}", orderId, attempt)` runs with orderId = 42 and attempt = 3. Which properties are stored?
choices: Attempt = 42 and OrderId = 3
Attempt = 3 and OrderId = 42, matched by name
None: the call throws because the names differ
Only the text, since names are case-sensitive
quiz.explanation: Template placeholders take the arguments in order. The names in braces only label the properties, and the logger never sees your variable names, so it cannot match by name, and nothing throws: the entry is well formed and wrong. Keep the arguments in placeholder order, or let the [LoggerMessage] generator bind by parameter name at compile time.

quiz.prompt: A payment provider call fails, the automatic retry succeeds, and the customer is charged once. Which level fits the line about the failed first attempt?
choices: Critical, because payments matter to the business
Error, because an exception was thrown and caught
Warning: unexpected, but the code handled it
Debug, because the user never noticed anything
quiz.explanation: A level tells the reader what to do. Nothing failed for the customer, so an Error line would send someone to investigate an operation that succeeded, and Critical is for an app or dependency that is down. A handled surprise still deserves a trace in production, which Debug would not leave under the usual Information minimum; a rising count of these lines is the early signal of a struggling provider.

quiz.prompt: The minimum level is Information. What happens on `logger.LogDebug("Cart {Cart}", BuildCartDump())`?
choices: BuildCartDump runs, then the entry is dropped
BuildCartDump never runs, since the call is skipped
The entry is written, since Debug ranks above Information
The call throws, since Debug is switched off
quiz.explanation: C# evaluates every argument before a method body runs, and the level check happens inside the logger, so the dump is built and then thrown away. The compiler skips nothing, Debug ranks below Information, and a disabled level is silent rather than an exception. Guard an expensive argument with logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug) when it really must be logged.

quiz.prompt: Middleware wraps `await next(context)` in a `BeginScope` holding a CorrelationId. A repository logs three calls deeper, after several awaits. What does its line carry?
choices: Nothing extra, because a scope ends at the first await
The CorrelationId only in lines the middleware writes itself
A fresh CorrelationId generated for each class that logs
The CorrelationId, when the provider includes scopes
quiz.explanation: The scope sits in an async-local slot that flows with the execution context, so it survives awaits and reaches every logger used during the request until the using block ends. It is not tied to the class that opened it, and nothing generates new ids. Whether you see it depends on the provider: the console formatter prints scopes only with IncludeScopes set.

quiz.prompt: A handler calls `logger.LogInformation("Login attempt {Request}", request)`, where `request` is a `record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password)`. What does the message show?
choices: Only the type name, LoginRequest
Every property, the password too
The email only, since Password is a sensitive name
Nothing, since objects are skipped
quiz.explanation: The default formatter renders an object argument with ToString(), and a record's compiler-generated ToString prints each property as Name = value, so the password lands in clear text. Nothing in Microsoft.Extensions.Logging guesses which names are sensitive, and objects are not dropped. Log chosen fields, such as a user id and an outcome, instead of the whole object.

quiz.prompt: A sign-in fails. Which log line is safe to keep for months?
choices: `Sign-in failed for {Email} with password {Password}`
`Sign-in failed; request body {Body}`
`Sign-in failed; Authorization header {Authorization}`
`Sign-in failed for {UserId}: {Reason}`
quiz.explanation: A stable user id and a reason code such as bad-password let you count attacks and help one person without storing anything secret. A wrong password is often a typo of the real one, the body carries that same password, and the Authorization header is a credential that anyone reading the logs could replay. An email is personal data, so it needs a reason of its own.

quiz.prompt: A team hides the headers Authorization and Cookie and logs every other request header. A partner starts sending `X-Api-Key`. What ends up in the log?
choices: Nothing: the key is redacted, since it looks secret
Nothing: the logging middleware rejects the request
The partner's API key, in clear text
Only the header name, with its value dropped
quiz.explanation: A deny-list hides only the names somebody wrote down, so a new credential header is logged as it arrives. No logger inspects values to guess what is secret, and logging never rejects requests. An allow-list fails closed: log the headers you know are safe and write the rest as [Redacted], which is how ASP.NET Core's HTTP logging treats headers outside its RequestHeaders set.

quiz.prompt: A catch block logs a failed payment. Which call stores the stack trace in the entry's exception field?
choices: `logger.LogError(ex, "Payment {PaymentId} failed", paymentId)`
`logger.LogError("Payment {PaymentId} failed", paymentId, ex)`
`logger.LogError("Payment failed: {Error}", ex.Message)`
`logger.LogError($"Payment {paymentId} failed: {ex}")`
quiz.explanation: Only the overload with an Exception parameter fills that field, where the provider keeps type, message and stack trace. Appended after paymentId, ex is a surplus template argument with no placeholder, so the field stays empty. Logging ex.Message drops the stack trace, and the interpolated version also turns the template into one-off text.

quiz.prompt: Startup logs the full `ConnectionStrings:Orders` value so that on-call can see which server the app uses. What is the safer line?
choices: The same value at Debug, which production never turns on
The same value base64-encoded, so nobody reads it at a glance
The same value, but only once at startup
The server and database names parsed from it
quiz.explanation: A connection string usually carries a password or key, and anyone who can read the logs could then reach the database. Parsing it with DbConnectionStringBuilder and logging only the host and database answers the on-call question. Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse, a Debug line is one config change away from production, and a single startup line is still kept for months.

flashcards.back: Log text with named holes such as {OrderId}: the text stays fixed across calls and each value is stored beside it under that name.
Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical; None switches a category off.
Error: one operation failed and needs a look. Critical: the app or a whole dependency is down and someone must act now.
Says whether a level would be written for this category; check it before computing an argument that costs real work.
The console formatter option that prints scope values; it is off by default, so scopes seem to vanish in a plain console.
One id per request, taken from an incoming header or generated, echoed in the response and attached to each log line through a scope.
Emails, names, addresses and IPs are personal data; logs are copied and kept for months, so prefer a stable internal id.
A source generator attribute on a partial method: it checks the level before boxing values and matches placeholders to parameters at build time.

topics.title: Background work & graceful shutdown
topics.summary: A BackgroundService loop over a stopping token, a bounded Channel between requests and the worker, a per-job catch that tells a failed job from a shutdown, stopping in order (refuse new work, drain until the deadline, hand the rest back), PeriodicTimer for periodic work, and why async void and fire-and-forget Task.Run from a request lose work.

quiz.prompt: The app is shutting down. What does the host do with the `stoppingToken` it passed to a `BackgroundService`'s `ExecuteAsync`?
choices: Nothing; the worker thread is aborted at process exit
Cancels it, then waits up to the shutdown timeout
Cancels it and returns at once, while the loop keeps running
Disposes the worker first, then cancels the token
quiz.explanation: StopAsync on a BackgroundService cancels the token and then awaits the task that ExecuteAsync returned, so a loop that honours the token can finish its current job. The wait is bounded by HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, 30 seconds by default. .NET never aborts threads, and services are disposed only after the hosted services have been stopped.

quiz.prompt: An `ExecuteAsync` loop awaits `handler.Handle(job)` with no try/catch, and one job throws. With the default host options on .NET 10, what happens?
choices: The job is retried until it succeeds
The exception is logged and the next job runs
The worker ends and the host stops the app
Nothing visible: the host swallows the exception
quiz.explanation: The exception faults the task that ExecuteAsync returned, and BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior defaults to StopHost, so the host logs the error and shuts the whole app down. Nothing retries the job, and the next job never runs because the loop is gone. With Ignore the process stays up without a worker; a per-job try/catch is the real fix.

quiz.prompt: A bounded channel created with capacity 100 and `FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait` holds 100 jobs. What does a request's `await writer.WriteAsync(job)` do?
choices: Throws ChannelClosedException, since the channel is full
Drops the oldest queued job to make room
Waits until the worker reads a job and frees a slot
Grows past 100, since Wait only applies to readers
quiz.explanation: Wait is backpressure: the write completes only when a reader takes an item and a slot opens, so a slow worker slows the producers instead of growing memory. Dropping the oldest item is the DropOldest mode, ChannelClosedException is for a completed channel, and the capacity limits writers. In a request, TryWrite is often better: it returns false at once and lets you answer 503.

quiz.prompt: An endpoint runs `_ = Task.Run(() => SendReceiptAsync(order, db))` with the request's DbContext and returns 202. What goes wrong?
choices: Task.Run cannot start an async lambda, so it will not compile
The context may be disposed first, and shutdown does not wait
The 202 response waits until the receipt has actually been sent
The receipt runs twice, once per thread
quiz.explanation: The request scope, and the DbContext in it, is disposed once the request ends, so the background task can hit ObjectDisposedException halfway. The host does not track the task either, so a deploy cuts it off, and its exceptions go unobserved. Task.Run accepts async lambdas and returns at once, so the 202 is not delayed. Queue a job for a worker that owns its own scope.

quiz.prompt: A timer callback is declared `async void OnTick()`, and one tick throws. What happens?
choices: It is rethrown on the thread pool and ends the process
The exception is stored in a Task that nobody ever awaits
The timer logs the exception and keeps ticking
Nothing, since an async void method cannot throw
quiz.explanation: An async void method returns no Task, so there is nowhere to store the exception. The async machinery rethrows it on the captured context, which in a console or ASP.NET Core app is the thread pool, and an unhandled thread-pool exception terminates the process. Timers do not catch it for you. Return Task and await it, or catch inside the method.

quiz.prompt: A `PeriodicTimer` has a 10-second period, and one run of the work takes 25 seconds. What happens next?
choices: Two extra runs start in parallel so the schedule catches up
The two missed ticks run back to back, then the schedule resumes
The timer stops for good, because two of its ticks were missed
The next wait returns at once; runs never overlap
quiz.explanation: A PeriodicTimer remembers at most one pending tick. The ticks that passed during the 25-second run collapse into one, so the next WaitForNextTickAsync completes immediately, and later ticks keep the original rhythm. Nothing runs in parallel, because the loop awaits the work before it waits again, and missed ticks neither queue up nor stop the timer.

quiz.prompt: At shutdown a worker still has 40 jobs in its in-memory channel and 30 seconds left. Which stop loses nothing?
choices: Return at once, since in-memory jobs are cheap to lose
Keep working until the queue is empty, however long it takes
Clear the channel so the next start begins from a clean state
Refuse new jobs, drain to the deadline, hand back the rest
quiz.explanation: Completing the writer stops new work while the queued items stay readable. Draining uses the shutdown window, and whatever is left, including a job cut off mid-run, goes to durable storage for a retry. Working until the queue is empty ignores the deadline, so the orchestrator kills the process mid-job, and clearing or abandoning the channel silently drops customer work.

quiz.prompt: A periodic loop is `while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))`. What does the wait do when the host cancels `stoppingToken`?
choices: Throws OperationCanceledException, which ends the loop
Returns false, so the while condition ends the loop normally
Returns true one last time so the body runs, then false
Keeps waiting until the next tick arrives, ignoring the token
quiz.explanation: A cancelled token cancels the pending wait, so it throws; returning false is what a disposed timer does. The exception that leaves ExecuteAsync during a stop is expected: the host completes its shutdown without reporting a failure. Catch it only to run cleanup, and never swallow it in a way that keeps the loop alive.

quiz.prompt: After `writer.Complete()`, a worker runs `await foreach (var job in reader.ReadAllAsync())` on a channel that still holds 5 jobs. What happens?
choices: The loop ends at once and the 5 jobs are lost
It yields all 5 jobs, then the loop ends
It throws ChannelClosedException before the first job
It waits forever for a sixth job that never comes
quiz.explanation: Completing a channel closes it for writers only. Readers still receive everything already queued, and ReadAllAsync finishes once the channel is both completed and empty, which is how a drain knows it is done. ChannelClosedException is what a WriteAsync after Complete throws, and waiting forever is what happens when nobody completes the writer.

quiz.prompt: Which per-job catch lets a worker survive any failing job, a timed-out one included, and still stop promptly on shutdown?
choices: `catch (Exception) { }` around the whole loop
`catch (OperationCanceledException) { continue; }`
`catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException) { }`
`catch (Exception ex) when (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)`
quiz.explanation: The stopping token is the only witness of a shutdown: while it is not cancelled, every exception, a job's own OperationCanceledException included, is a job failure to log. Filtering on the exception type lets a timed-out job's cancellation escape and end the worker. Catching only cancellations lets ordinary failures through, and a catch around the whole loop ends it at the first bad job.

flashcards.back: The long-running method of a hosted worker; it receives a token that is cancelled when the host begins to stop.
How long the host gives its hosted services to stop before it moves on: 30 seconds by default.
What a full bounded channel does with a new item: Wait (the default), DropOldest, DropNewest or DropWrite.

flashcards.front: TryWrite on a full bounded channel
flashcards.back: Returns false at once instead of waiting, so an endpoint can answer 503 or 429 rather than hold the request open.
A singleton worker creates a scope from IServiceScopeFactory for each job, so scoped services such as a DbContext live only as long as that job.
An async timer for a single consumer: await WaitForNextTickAsync in a loop; disposing the timer makes the wait return false.

flashcards.front: When is an in-memory queue not enough?
flashcards.back: When the work must happen: the channel dies with the process, so a crash or deploy loses its items. Use a durable queue or an outbox table.

flashcards.front: Why not Thread.Sleep in a worker loop?
flashcards.back: It blocks a thread-pool thread and ignores the stopping token, so a stop waits out the whole sleep. Await Task.Delay(period, stoppingToken) or a PeriodicTimer instead.

topics.title: System.Text.Json as an API contract
topics.summary: Why a DTO and not the entity is the contract, naming policies and [JsonPropertyName], case-insensitive reading, refusing unknown members, required members and null handling, enums as names, numbers and dates that survive the round trip, and polymorphic DTOs with [JsonDerivedType].
topics.lesson:
## The DTO is the contract, not the entity

Clients depend on the exact JSON you send and accept. Serializing an EF entity ties that JSON to the database: every public property goes out (a `PasswordHash` included), a request bound to the entity sets any property the client names (`"isAdmin": true`, which is over-posting), and a navigation property that points back to its parent throws `JsonException: A possible object cycle was detected`. A DTO lists the fields of the contract and nothing else, so a renamed column stays an internal change. Map the entity to the DTO in one place and test the DTO's JSON.

## Names: naming policy and [JsonPropertyName]

`new JsonSerializerOptions()` writes names as declared (`OrderId`) and reads them case-sensitively, so `{"orderId":7}` binds nothing and `OrderId` silently keeps its default. `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` switches on camelCase names, case-insensitive reading and numbers sent as strings; ASP.NET Core uses those defaults for minimal APIs and controllers, but a console tool or a test that creates its own options does not. A `[JsonPropertyName("placed_at")]` is the final name in both directions: the naming policy applies only to properties without one.

```csharp
var json = new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);   // create once, reuse everywhere
```

## Reading: unknown, required and null members

By default a member the DTO does not have is skipped silently, which also hides a typo such as `custmer`. Set `UnmappedMemberHandling = JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow` (or put `[JsonUnmappedMemberHandling]` on the type) to get a `JsonException` instead. A C# `required` member, or one marked `[JsonRequired]`, must appear in the JSON, while a missing plain `int` simply stays 0. `required` does not reject an explicit `null`: `{"customer":null}` is accepted for a `required string` until you set `RespectNullableAnnotations = true`.

## Writing: nulls, defaults and enums

`DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull` leaves out null properties. `WhenWritingDefault` also drops 0, `false` and the enum member with value 0, so a client cannot tell "zero items" from "unknown". Enums are written as numbers unless you add `JsonStringEnumConverter`, used by the `dotnet-stripe` sample's `ConfigureHttpJsonOptions`. The converter reads names case-insensitively and refuses an unknown name, but it still accepts any number, 99 included, unless you pass `allowIntegerValues: false`:

```csharp
json.Converters.Add(new JsonStringEnumConverter(JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase, allowIntegerValues: false));
```

## Numbers and dates

`decimal` keeps its scale: `12.50m` is written as `12.50` and reads back exactly. A `long` such as 9007199254740993 is written with every digit, but a browser's `JSON.parse` turns it into a double and gets 9007199254740992, because a double holds every integer only up to 2^53. Send large ids as strings, or set `NumberHandling = JsonNumberHandling.WriteAsString`. Dates are ISO 8601 text: a `DateTimeOffset` carries its offset, a `DateTime` with `Kind = Utc` ends in `Z`, and an `Unspecified` one has no offset at all, so each side guesses. `DateOnly` is written as `2026-11-15`.

## Polymorphism with [JsonDerivedType]

```csharp
[JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "kind")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(CardPaymentDto), "card")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(BankPaymentDto), "bank")]
abstract record PaymentDto;
```

The discriminator is written, first, only when the serializer is asked for the base type: `Serialize<PaymentDto>(card)` gives `{"kind":"card",...}`, while `Serialize(card)` with a variable typed `CardPaymentDto` writes no kind at all. Without `TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName` the property is called `$type`. Reading the base type with an unknown kind throws a `JsonException`, and a missing kind throws `NotSupportedException`. The kind must be the first property unless `AllowOutOfOrderMetadataProperties = true`.

quiz.prompt: A team returns its EF `User` entity from GET /users/{id} and also accepts it as the body of PUT /users/{id}. Which risk comes from that choice?
choices: System.Text.Json cannot serialize EF Core entities at all
Responses get slower, because entities serialize every byte twice
PasswordHash goes out, and a client can send IsAdmin: true
Only the property names change, which clients can absorb
quiz.explanation: The serializer writes every public property, so the hash leaves the server, and binding a request to the entity sets any property the client names, which is over-posting. Serializing an entity works and costs no extra time; navigation properties even add cycles that throw. A DTO lists exactly the fields of the contract, so a schema change stays internal.

quiz.prompt: `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order>("{\"orderId\":7}")` runs with no options, and `Order` has a property `OrderId`. What is `OrderId` afterwards?
choices: 0, with no error
7, because names match case-insensitively
A JsonException for the unknown member
7, because camelCase is the default policy
quiz.explanation: Plain options compare property names case-sensitively and skip members they cannot map, so orderId matches nothing and the property keeps its default. Case-insensitive reading and camelCase names come from JsonSerializerDefaults.Web, which ASP.NET Core uses for you; a console tool or a test that creates its own options gets neither.

quiz.prompt: A property is declared `[JsonPropertyName("placed_at")] public DateTimeOffset PlacedAt`, and the options use `JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase`. Which name is used on the wire?
choices: placedAt, because the policy wins
placed_at when writing, placedAt when reading
PlacedAt, because the attribute switches the policy off for the whole type
placed_at, both ways
quiz.explanation: An explicit [JsonPropertyName] is the final name: the naming policy applies only to properties without one, and the same name serves reading and writing. The other properties of the type still get camelCase. That makes the attribute the tool for one legacy field and the policy the tool for everything else.

quiz.prompt: A client sends `{"id":7,"customer":"ana","isAdmin":true}` to an endpoint whose DTO has no IsAdmin property. With default options, what happens to isAdmin?
choices: Deserialization fails with a JsonException
It is skipped, and nobody hears about it
It is stored in an extension-data dictionary
The request is answered with 400 automatically
quiz.explanation: System.Text.Json passes over members it cannot map unless told otherwise, which also hides typos such as custmer. Set UnmappedMemberHandling to Disallow, in the options or with the attribute on the type, to get a JsonException instead. Extension data needs a [JsonExtensionData] property on the DTO, and since reading succeeds, nothing answers 400.

quiz.prompt: A DTO declares `public required string Customer { get; init; }`. The JSON is `{"customer":null}`, read with the Web defaults of .NET 10. What happens?
choices: JsonException: a required member is missing
It is accepted, and Customer is null
Customer becomes an empty string
The compiler rejects the DTO, since required needs a non-null default
quiz.explanation: required only checks that the property appears in the JSON, and here it does. A null for a non-nullable reference type passes unless the options set RespectNullableAnnotations, an opt-in flag that then throws. The compiler cannot see JSON, and the serializer never invents an empty string, so the null lands in a property your code believes is never null.

quiz.prompt: The options set `DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingDefault`. An order has `Quantity = 0` and `Status = Placed`, the first enum value. What does the client receive?
choices: Both values, since only nulls are left out
Quantity 0 and no Status
An exception, because 0 is not a valid quantity value
Neither: both equal their default and are left out
quiz.explanation: WhenWritingDefault drops every property equal to default(T): null for references, 0 for numbers, false for bools and the enum member whose value is 0. A client that treats a missing field as unknown then cannot tell that the order was placed with zero items. WhenWritingNull leaves out only nulls, the safe choice for a contract.

quiz.prompt: An API adds `new JsonStringEnumConverter()`, and a client sends `"status": 99`. What happens?
choices: It is accepted as the undefined value 99
JsonException: 99 is not a defined status
It is read as the enum's first value
It is read as the closest defined value
quiz.explanation: The converter writes names, but by default it still reads integers, and a C# enum holds any value of its underlying type, so (Status)99 reaches your code. Pass allowIntegerValues: false to refuse numbers, and check Enum.IsDefined where the value matters. An unknown name such as "lost" is refused; reading never picks the first or a nearby member.

quiz.prompt: An order id is a `long` of 9007199254740993, and a browser reads the JSON with `JSON.parse`. What does the client get?
choices: 9007199254740993, since JSON numbers are exact
A JsonException, written by the server
9007199254740992: past 2^53 a double cannot hold every integer
A string, because System.Text.Json quotes numbers above int.MaxValue
quiz.explanation: The server writes the exact digits, but JSON.parse turns every number into an IEEE double with a 53-bit mantissa, so the nearest representable value wins. System.Text.Json never quotes numbers on its own: opt in with NumberHandling set to WriteAsString, or make large ids strings in the contract, when browsers are clients.

quiz.prompt: A `DateTime` with `Kind = Unspecified` is serialized and read by a client in another time zone. What is the problem?
choices: System.Text.Json refuses to write an Unspecified DateTime
The value is written as a Unix timestamp in seconds
It is converted to UTC using the server's local time zone
No offset is written, so the client must guess the zone
quiz.explanation: An Unspecified DateTime goes out as 2026-11-15T09:30:00 with nothing after it, and it reads back as Unspecified too, so each side applies its own assumption. A Utc DateTime gets a trailing Z, and a DateTimeOffset carries its offset. The serializer neither converts nor refuses the value, and it writes ISO 8601 text, not epoch numbers.

quiz.prompt: `PaymentDto` carries `[JsonDerivedType(typeof(CardPaymentDto), "card")]`. Code runs `var card = new CardPaymentDto(...); JsonSerializer.Serialize(card)`. Is "card" written as the discriminator?
choices: Yes, because the attribute is always applied
No: the static type is CardPaymentDto, not the base
Yes, but only when the derived type is sealed
No, because records cannot be polymorphic
quiz.explanation: Polymorphism is configured on the base type and used only when the serializer is asked for that type: Serialize<PaymentDto>(card) writes kind first, while Serialize(card) infers the derived type and writes plain properties. Records and classes behave the same here, and sealing changes nothing. Type the variable or the endpoint's return value as PaymentDto.

flashcards.back: camelCase property names, case-insensitive reading and numbers accepted in quotes; ASP.NET Core applies it to minimal APIs and controllers.
Turns a JSON member without a matching property into a JsonException; set it in the options or as an attribute on one type.
The serializer throws a JsonException when that property is absent from the JSON; a plain property just keeps its default.
An options flag that makes null in a non-nullable reference property a JsonException, when reading and when writing.
The JsonStringEnumConverter argument that refuses 1 and "1" alike, so only member names get in.
First in the object by default; AllowOutOfOrderMetadataProperties = true lets a client put it anywhere.

flashcards.front: Reading a polymorphic base: kind problems
flashcards.back: A kind that no [JsonDerivedType] declares is a JsonException; no kind at all on an abstract base is a NotSupportedException.
It leaks internal columns, invites over-posting on input, throws on navigation cycles and ties the API to the database schema.
